title: The little way
hookLine: Thérèse of Lisieux finds holiness in small things done with great love

cards: Dirty water keeps landing on a young nun's face. She's at the laundry tubs in a convent in Lisieux, in France, and the sister beside her is scrubbing so hard the spray flies every time.
The young nun wants to step back and wipe her face. Instead, she decides to stand there and take it as a small gift. She tells it herself, in her memoir.
It's not a dramatic story. That's the point. Her name is Thérèse, and she spent the rest of her short life inside those convent walls, finding a way to God made of moments like this.

teach.b: Thérèse read about the great saints and felt like a grain of sand next to a mountain.

teach.h: A LIFT INSTEAD OF A CLIMB.
teach.b: In her memoir, later published as Story of a Soul, she says she was too small to climb the steep stairway of perfection. So she looked for another way up.
She lived in a time of new inventions, and she pictured an elevator: something that carries you up when you can't climb. She found it in two lines of scripture.
Proverbs, in the Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." And Isaiah: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you."
The lift, she decided, was being carried: not climbing harder, but staying small and letting God's arms do the lifting.
Jesus says something close in Matthew, in the King James Bible: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." In a day, it looked like this.
A smile for a sister who got on her nerves. Not answering back. Letting the water hit her face.
She described these as flowers she could scatter, small things no one would notice, done with as much love as she could put into them. Thérèse died young, inside the same convent.
The Catholic Church later named her a saint and a Doctor of the Church, a title for teachers whose writing is trusted to guide the whole Church.
Christians outside the Catholic Church read her book too, and find laundry tubs, chores and small kindnesses.

how: Catholics keep Thérèse's feast day and read Story of a Soul, and some Christians take up her little way by offering ordinary tasks and small kindnesses to God through the day.

s: Thérèse became well-known for great public works
she lived inside a convent and wrote about small, hidden acts done with love.
she pictured her way to God as a lift, or elevator
too small to climb the stairway, she wanted to be carried.
the little way means aiming low
it means doing small things with great love, and trusting God like a child.

games.q: you're at the laundry tubs, and the sister beside you keeps splashing dirty water in your face. what do you do?
o: tell her to be more careful.
stay where you are and take it as a small gift.
games.why: Thérèse tells it herself: she wanted to step back, and instead she stayed, and welcomed the splashes.

practice: Look for the smallest, dullest job in your day: folding laundry, a reply to an email, listening to a story you've heard before. Picture doing it slowly and carefully, as if for someone you love, knowing probably no one will see.
If you pray, offer it to God before you start, the way Thérèse did.

wordCard.voice: Lisieux. The French convent town where a young nun found God not by climbing higher but by staying small, in laundry tubs and hidden kindnesses.

carryVoice: Your line: small things, great love. Nobody has to notice for it to count. That's day nine hundred thirty-six.
